content.comment_body: I'm looking to set up a test system for heater blocks containing 5x 300W heaters. I want to convert the resistance values of the heaters into an analog input to verify if they are within tolerance. Using a thermocouple to check the block temperature doesn't help identify individual faulty elements, and there are health and safety risks when handling hot metal blocks in the workshop. Thanks for any advice.
The easiest way is to purchase a multimeter to perform resistance measurements.

We handle large quantities of heaters daily, all using Harting connectors. My goal was to design a test box for engineers where they could simply plug in the heaters, press a button, and confirm they are functioning correctly. I work in a factory that deals with injection molding and extrusion, so this would help decrease the workload for the team.

For the [product_name], there is no module available to directly measure resistance; only voltage signals (0-10V) or current signals (0/4-20mA) can be processed. If your [product_name] base module doesn't have analog inputs, you'll need an analog expansion module like AM2. You could then set up a voltage divider using a suitable series resistor with the device under test. Connect the divider, for example, to 24 VDC, and measure the voltage across the test object in parallel.

analysis.insight_summary: The user is aiming to automate heater block resistance testing by converting resistance readings into analog signals for batch checks. The limitation mentioned is the absence of direct resistance measurement in [product_name] modules, prompting the use of analog voltage or current inputs as workarounds. The discussion centers on streamlining manual tasks and boosting efficiency in a factory setting.
